query: For additively manufactured high-entropy-alloy components, what single intervention could improve dimensional precision and mechanical integrity while reducing fabrication-induced defects? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the current fabrication baseline, defines the processing and application conditions under which it should hold, identifies supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing the effective laser energy density during selective laser melting (SLM) of refractory high-entropy alloys will reduce the formation of undissolved high-melting components, minimize cracking and porosity, and thereby improve both dimensional precision and mechanical integrity of additively manufactured parts.
generation.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured refractory HEA components (e.g., NbMoTaW or similar compositions) fabricated via SLM that show processing defects such as undissolved high-melting phases (e.g., tungsten), cracks, and porosity.
generation.intervention: Increase the volumetric laser energy input (via optimizing laser power, scan speed, and hatch spacing) to ensure complete melting and homogeneous mixing of all constituent elements.
generation.conditions: This intervention should be applied during SLM processing of refractory high-entropy alloys with significant differences in melting points among elements, under processing conditions where current parameters lead to residual defects (e.g., using linear energy densities near or below ~2.83 J/mm as a baseline). The optimization should avoid excessive overheating that might cause other types of defects.
generation.structural_mediator: A more uniform, fully melted microstructure with reduced undissolved particles and fewer cracks/pores.
generation.mechanism: Increasing laser energy density enhances the complete melting and mixing of constituents with high melting points, reducing the formation of undissolved particles and residual stresses. This promotes finer, more homogeneous microstructures that improve dimensional stability during solidification and enhance mechanical performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the current baseline, the improved process is expected to yield components with tighter dimensional tolerances, a reduction in fabrication-induced microstructural defects, and enhanced mechanical properties (e.g., higher yield strength and ductility). The magnitude of improvements is uncertain and likely dependent on the specific alloy system and process window.
generation.baseline: SLM-fabricated refractory HEA components produced under current parameter sets that yield noticeable defects such as undissolved high-melting particles and associated microcracking.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for SLM processing of HEAs containing elements with markedly differing melting points under similar thermal gradients; its applicability to other additive manufacturing techniques or different alloy systems remains to be verified.
generation.uncertainty: The exact optimum energy density and related SLM parameters will vary with the particular HEA composition and machine setup. Additionally, over-melting may introduce new defects such as keyholing or excessive residual stresses; therefore, fine-tuning is needed.

falsification_experiment.design: Process a series of identical refractory HEA samples using SLM under controlled variations of laser energy density. One group is processed using the current baseline settings, while other groups are processed with incrementally increased laser energy density. All other parameters (scan speed, hatch spacing, etc.) are held constant. Post-fabrication, assess dimensional tolerances, defect populations (via microscopy), and mechanical properties (via tensile and compression tests).
measurements: Quantitative dimensional precision (e.g., deviation from CAD dimensions)
Defect density and type (e.g., porosity, undissolved particles, cracks) using SEM and X-ray CT
Mechanical integrity metrics (yield strength, tensile ductility, hardness) through mechanical testing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If samples processed with increased laser energy density do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in dimensional accuracy and mechanical properties, or if they display new or exacerbated defects (e.g., keyholing or thermal-induced distortions) relative to the baseline, then the hypothesis that increased laser energy density is beneficial will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) have excellent mechanical properties, which could make them the substitutes of some superalloys. However, the high melting point of refractory HEAs leads to processing problems when using traditional processing techniques. In this study, a single BCC solid solution of NbMoTaW alloy was formed by selective laser melting (SLM) with a linear energy density of up to 2.83 J/mm. The composition distribution was analyzed, and the element with a lower melting point and lower density showed a negative deviation (no more than 5%) of the molar ratio in the formed alloy. The HEA shows an excellent microstructure, microhardness, and corrosion resistance performance compared with traditional superalloys, making it a new substitute metal with great application prospects in aerospace and energy fields.

These are essentially cracks, mostly perpendicular to the build direction, and undissolved particles. PBF-LB/M A results in considerably smaller cracks than PBF-LB/M B but contains undissolved powder particles which were identified as tungsten particles by EDS measurements. Tungsten has the highest melting point of the alloy’s elements [ [26] ] and consequently is the hardest to dissolve during PBF-LB/M.
